newsitem.title: USA: Dell makes inroads selling via Internet.
newsitem.headline: Dell makes inroads selling via Internet.

text.p: Dell Computer Corp - the company that pioneered the direct selling model in PCs - said the industry is "moving in its direction," with the Internet representing the ultimate extension of its direct sales model.

Dell executives, who were hosting an analyst meeting here, said that Dell is having great success in selling PCs over the Internet. It is getting about $5 million in revenues a week at its Web site, as customers build their own machines.
"The Internet is the ultimate extension of the direct model," said Dell Chief Financial Officer Tom Meredith.

Dell executives said that they would hope that eventually, 100 percent of all of their customer transactions would be done via the Internet, which they said also have higher average sales prices and richer profit margins.
But for now, analysts said at the current rate, Dell could see about $200-$300 million in revenues this fiscal year from the Internet, and eventually up to $1 billion in sales.

Dell officials said that the Internet is a great low-cost platform for selling because it is almost like letting customers having a window onto the factory floor, as they configure a custom system, via a point and click of the mouse.

Dell executives also said that another example of the industry moving to its direct model was the recent confirmation that Compaq Computer Corp approached direct seller Micron Electronics Inc about a merger, even though Micron said the two are no longer in talks.

"We would be quite excited about that happening," Meredith said. He added that while he was not convinced Compaq would buy Micron Electronics, or as was also rumored, Gateway 2000 Inc, the fact that their fierce PC rival Compaq has been investigating the direct sales model, validates their business strategy.
Compaq and other PC makers sell their systems through retailers, distributors and resellers who sometimes repackage the PCs and provide services to smaller and medium businesses.
But Dell also plans to expand its service offerings as well, beyond its five offerings which include a recent deal to offer more direct financing through a new leasing partner.

"Imagine two ends of a railroad track, Compaq is on one end and Dell is on the other," said Louis Mazzucchelli, a Gerard Klauer Mattison analyst. "These two trains are heading toward each other on this track and the question is, where are they going to meet and who is going to be the bigger train."
